new.stem: A 28-year-old woman, a smoker with five children (all breast-fed), has had bloody nipple discharge from the right breast for 6 months. At times the area swells with a foul-smelling discharge; antibiotics did not help. Tests show mildly dilated multiple lactiferous ducts. What is the management?
new.explanation: Duct ectasia/periductal mastitis is benign: reassure, stop smoking and follow up; total duct excision only for persistent discharge or recurrent sepsis.

new.stem: A 28-year-old woman, a smoker with five children (all breast-fed), has had bloody nipple discharge from the right breast for 6 months. At times the area swells with a foul-smelling discharge; antibiotics did not help. Which of the following is NOT useful in investigating her condition?
new.explanation: Triple assessment (examination, ultrasound/mammography, cytology) suffices; MRI adds nothing in benign duct ectasia.

new.stem: A 28-year-old woman, a smoker with five children (all breast-fed), has had bloody nipple discharge from the right breast for 6 months. At times the area swells with a foul-smelling discharge; antibiotics did not help. What is the diagnosis?
new.explanation: Smoking, multiparity and multiple dilated ducts with discharge and recurrent periareolar inflammation are typical of duct ectasia/periductal mastitis.

new.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a 3-month painless lump in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast and nipple retraction for 2 weeks. Core biopsy of a palpable axillary node shows invasive carcinoma, hormone-receptor negative; PET shows no metastasis. What is the best next step in management?
new.explanation: Node-positive cancer with nipple involvement needs mastectomy with axillary clearance; neoadjuvant chemotherapy is often given first for ER-negative disease.

new.stem: 8 months after her surgery she has difficulty raising her arm and her medial scapula is prominent. What is the cause?
options: Tear of the long head of biceps
new.explanation: Winging of the scapula follows injury to the long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior) during axillary dissection; thoracodorsal injury weakens latissimus dorsi.

new.stem: An elderly man with previous bloody stools and lower abdominal pain has a sudden attack of left iliac fossa pain with fever. Ultrasound shows thickening of the sigmoid colon. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: LIF pain, fever and sigmoid wall thickening in an older patient is acute diverticulitis.

new.stem: An elderly man with previous bloody stools and lower abdominal pain has a sudden attack of left iliac fossa pain with fever. Ultrasound shows thickening of the sigmoid colon. What is the best investigation now?
new.explanation: Contrast CT confirms diverticulitis and shows abscess or perforation; colonoscopy and barium enema are avoided acutely (perforation risk).

new.stem: An elderly man with previous bloody stools and lower abdominal pain has a sudden attack of left iliac fossa pain with fever. Ultrasound shows thickening of the sigmoid colon. What is the treatment?
new.explanation: Uncomplicated diverticulitis is treated conservatively (bowel rest, fluids, antibiotics if systemically unwell); drainage is for abscess > 4 cm.

items.stem: A woman with an anal fissure in whom conservative management has failed.
items.explanation: After failed topical therapy, botulinum toxin is preferred in women (obstetric sphincter risk); lateral sphincterotomy is used in men or if Botox fails.

items.stem: A patient with prolapsed haemorrhoids that need manual reduction or remain prolapsed.
items.explanation: Grade III–IV haemorrhoids are treated by excisional haemorrhoidectomy; stapled haemorrhoidopexy is an alternative for grade III.

items.stem: A man with fever and a fluctuant perianal mass.
items.explanation: A perianal abscess needs incision and drainage.

items.stem: A man with Crohn disease and a low fistula-in-ano.
items.explanation: Perianal Crohn fistulas are managed with a loose draining seton plus medical therapy to avoid incontinence and non-healing wounds.

items.stem: A woman with painless haemorrhoids that prolapse on defecation and reduce spontaneously.
items.explanation: Grade II haemorrhoids are treated by rubber band ligation.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis has massive haematemesis and hypotension. He has spider naevi and ascites.
items.explanation: Massive haematemesis with stigmata of chronic liver disease is bleeding oesophageal varices.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man vomits blood-streaked material after several bouts of forceful retching following heavy drinking. He is stable and the bleeding stops spontaneously.
items.explanation: Haematemesis after forceful retching that settles spontaneously is a Mallory–Weiss tear.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man taking NSAIDs for osteoarthritis has melaena and anaemia. He is otherwise healthy.
items.explanation: NSAID use with melaena and anaemia is a bleeding peptic ulcer.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman has fatigue and pallor and has neglected tarry stools for a year. There is a hard, non-tender lump above the left clavicle.
items.explanation: Chronic melaena with a left supraclavicular (Virchow) node is gastric cancer.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: An elderly woman in a care home who takes antipsychotics and has chronic constipation presents with a distended, painless, non-tender abdomen. X-ray shows a hugely dilated sigmoid loop reaching the upper abdomen. What is the diagnosis?
new.explanation: A huge sigmoid loop rising from the pelvis (coffee-bean sign) in an elderly, constipated, institutionalised patient is sigmoid volvulus.

new.stem: An elderly woman in a care home who takes antipsychotics and has chronic constipation presents with a distended, painless, non-tender abdomen. X-ray shows a hugely dilated sigmoid loop reaching the upper abdomen. Which procedure is both diagnostic and therapeutic?
new.explanation: Flexible sigmoidoscopy confirms the twist, checks viability and decompresses with a flatus tube; elective sigmoid colectomy follows to prevent recurrence.

new.stem: An elderly woman in a care home who takes antipsychotics and has chronic constipation presents with a distended, painless, non-tender abdomen. X-ray shows a hugely dilated sigmoid loop reaching the upper abdomen. At surgery the descending and sigmoid colon are resected. Which artery is ligated?
new.explanation: The descending and sigmoid colon are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery (left colic and sigmoid branches).

new.stem: A 21-year-old man has incapacitating perianal pain for 3 days despite local ointment. There is a tender, fluctuant right perianal swelling with overlying erythema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: A tender, fluctuant, erythematous swelling beside the anus is a perianal abscess.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: A 21-year-old man has incapacitating perianal pain for 3 days despite local ointment. There is a tender, fluctuant right perianal swelling with overlying erythema. What is the best treatment now?
new.explanation: An abscess needs prompt incision and drainage; antibiotics alone are inadequate.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: A 55-year-old man has had intermittent dysphagia for solids and liquids with central chest pain for 4 months. ECG and troponin are normal; sublingual nitrates relieve the pain. What is the diagnosis?
new.explanation: Intermittent dysphagia for solids and liquids with chest pain relieved by nitrates is diffuse oesophageal spasm (corkscrew oesophagus on barium).

new.stem: A 55-year-old man has had intermittent dysphagia for solids and liquids with central chest pain for 4 months. ECG and troponin are normal; sublingual nitrates relieve the pain. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
new.explanation: High-resolution manometry shows premature simultaneous contractions; endoscopy is done first to exclude obstruction.

new.stem: A 55-year-old man has had intermittent dysphagia for solids and liquids with central chest pain for 4 months. ECG and troponin are normal; sublingual nitrates relieve the pain. What is the best management now?
new.explanation: Oesophageal spasm is treated medically first (calcium channel blockers or nitrates); POEM is reserved for refractory cases.

items.stem: A 2-day-old infant with Down syndrome has projectile vomiting and a scaphoid abdomen. X-ray shows a double-bubble sign with no distal bowel gas.
items.explanation: Double bubble without distal gas in a baby with Down syndrome is duodenal atresia (vomiting is usually bilious if post-ampullary).

items.stem: A 2-week-old infant born at 28 weeks, in the NICU, develops sudden abdominal distension and bloody stool. X-ray shows gas in the bowel wall.
items.explanation: Pneumatosis intestinalis with distension and bloody stool in a preterm neonate is necrotising enterocolitis.

items.stem: A full-term 2-day-old has not passed meconium, vomits bile and is distended. Rectal examination produces an explosive release of gas and liquid stool.
items.explanation: Delayed meconium with an explosive decompression on rectal examination is Hirschsprung disease; rectal suction biopsy confirms it.

items.stem: A 5-day-old who was feeding well suddenly has bilious vomiting, tenderness and haemodynamic instability. Contrast shows the duodenojejunal flexure right of the spine with a corkscrew duodenum.
items.explanation: Bilious vomiting with an abnormally placed DJ flexure and corkscrew duodenum is malrotation with midgut volvulus: emergency Ladd procedure.

new.stem: An 18-month-old child, born at 34 weeks, has had a groin lump for 1 week that enlarges on coughing and disappears spontaneously. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: Paediatric inguinal hernias are almost always indirect, through a patent processus vaginalis; prematurity increases the risk.

new.stem: An 18-month-old child, born at 34 weeks, has had a groin lump for 1 week that enlarges on coughing and disappears spontaneously. What is the best investigation?
new.explanation: The diagnosis is clinical (history of a reducible lump with cough impulse); imaging is not needed.

new.stem: An 18-month-old child, born at 34 weeks, has had a groin lump for 1 week that enlarges on coughing and disappears spontaneously. What is the treatment?
new.explanation: Herniotomy (high ligation of the sac) is done soon after diagnosis because of the high incarceration risk; mesh is not used in children.

new.stem: A baby a few months old has feeding difficulty, with milk coming out of the nose during feeds, coughing and choking. There is no excessive salivation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: Nasal regurgitation of milk without drooling suggests a cleft (often submucous) palate; TOF presents at birth with excessive salivation.

new.stem: A baby a few months old has feeding difficulty, with milk coming out of the nose during feeds, coughing and choking. There is no excessive salivation. What is the optimal time of repair?
new.explanation: Cleft palate is repaired at about 6–12 months, before speech develops; cleft lip at about 3 months.

new.stem: A baby a few months old has feeding difficulty, with milk coming out of the nose during feeds, coughing and choking. There is no excessive salivation. Which is NOT a complication of this condition?
new.explanation: Cleft palate causes feeding and speech problems, otitis media (Eustachian dysfunction) and aspiration; it does not cause oesophageal stricture.

new.stem: An 18-hour-old girl born by spontaneous vaginal delivery has an imperforate anus with a rectovestibular fistula. She weighs 2750 g, looks healthy and has no associated defects. Initial management includes all of the following EXCEPT:
new.explanation: First 24 h: fluids, antibiotics, NG decompression and VACTERL screening; surgery is planned once the anatomy and associated anomalies are known.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: An 18-hour-old girl born by spontaneous vaginal delivery has an imperforate anus with a rectovestibular fistula. She weighs 2750 g, looks healthy and has no associated defects. What is the most appropriate operation?
new.explanation: A healthy girl with a vestibular fistula can have a primary single-stage PSARP; a colostomy is reserved for sick babies or high defects.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: A 12-hour-old boy has an imperforate anus with an absent anal dimple and is passing meconium in his urine. What is the next step?
new.explanation: Meconium in the urine means a rectourinary fistula (high lesion), so a diverting colostomy is done; imaging and waiting 24 h are for unclear cases.

new.stem: A 12-hour-old boy has an imperforate anus with an absent anal dimple and is passing meconium in his urine. How is the type of imperforate anus defined before definitive repair?
new.explanation: A high-pressure distal colostogram through the mucous fistula shows the rectal level and the fistula to the urinary tract.

new.stem: A 4-month-old boy with effortless (sometimes forceful) non-bilious vomiting, fever to 39.5 °C and 4–6 green diarrhoeal stools a day. All of the following are useful EXCEPT:
new.explanation: Fever with vomiting and diarrhoea suggests gastroenteritis; FBC, stool tests and ultrasound help, but barium follow-through has no role.

new.stem: A 4-month-old boy with effortless (sometimes forceful) non-bilious vomiting, fever to 39.5 °C and 4–6 green diarrhoeal stools a day. What is the diagnosis?
new.explanation: Fever, vomiting and diarrhoea point to infective (viral) gastroenteritis; pyloric stenosis causes vomiting without fever or diarrhoea.

new.stem: A 4-month-old boy with effortless (sometimes forceful) non-bilious vomiting, fever to 39.5 °C and 4–6 green diarrhoeal stools a day. What is the management?
new.explanation: Viral gastroenteritis is managed supportively with oral or IV rehydration; antibiotics and surgery have no role.

new.stem: A man has jaundice, weight loss and a cholestatic pattern (raised ALP and GGT). Ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic ducts, a collapsed gallbladder and a normal pancreas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: Dilated intrahepatic ducts with a collapsed gallbladder put the block above the cystic duct: hilar (Klatskin) cholangiocarcinoma.

new.stem: A man has jaundice, weight loss and a cholestatic pattern (raised ALP and GGT). Ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic ducts, a collapsed gallbladder and a normal pancreas. Which tumour marker is associated?
new.explanation: CA 19-9 is the marker for cholangiocarcinoma and pancreatic cancer (it is also raised by cholestasis itself).

new.stem: A man has jaundice, weight loss and a cholestatic pattern (raised ALP and GGT). Ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic ducts, a collapsed gallbladder and a normal pancreas. What causes the itching?
new.explanation: Pruritus in obstructive jaundice is due to retained bile salts (and other pruritogens) in the skin, not bilirubin.

new.stem: A man has jaundice, weight loss and a cholestatic pattern (raised ALP and GGT). Ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic ducts, a collapsed gallbladder and a normal pancreas. What is the best non-invasive investigation for diagnosis?
new.explanation: MRCP maps the biliary tree non-invasively and defines the level and extent of a hilar stricture before any drainage.

new.stem: A man has jaundice, weight loss and a cholestatic pattern (raised ALP and GGT). Ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic ducts, a collapsed gallbladder and a normal pancreas. The patient remains jaundiced after two ERCP attempts. What is the next step?
new.explanation: Hilar strictures that fail endoscopic stenting are drained percutaneously (PTC/PTBD).

new.stem: A man has fever, malaise and tender hepatomegaly after diarrhoea following travel to Nasiriyah. Ultrasound shows a 7-cm cystic liver lesion; blood cultures are negative. What is the most likely organism?
new.explanation: Fever, tender hepatomegaly and a liver abscess after dysentery with sterile blood cultures is an amoebic liver abscess.

new.stem: A man has fever, malaise and tender hepatomegaly after diarrhoea following travel to Nasiriyah. Ultrasound shows a 7-cm cystic liver lesion; blood cultures are negative. How did the organism reach the liver?
options: Haematogenous spread via the hepatic artery
Via the portal vein from the colon
Ascending infection via the bile duct
new.explanation: Trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa and travel in the portal venous blood to the liver (usually the right lobe).

new.stem: A man has fever, malaise and tender hepatomegaly after diarrhoea following travel to Nasiriyah. Ultrasound shows a 7-cm cystic liver lesion; blood cultures are negative. He receives a second-generation cephalosporin and metronidazole, and the cyst is aspirated. What does the aspirate show?
new.explanation: Amoebic abscess fluid is odourless, reddish-brown "anchovy sauce" (liquefied liver); pyogenic abscesses contain yellow pus.

new.stem: A man has fever, malaise and tender hepatomegaly after diarrhoea following travel to Nasiriyah. Ultrasound shows a 7-cm cystic liver lesion; blood cultures are negative. Which additional treatment is essential?
new.explanation: After metronidazole, a luminal amoebicide (diloxanide furoate or paromomycin) is needed to clear intestinal cysts and prevent relapse.

items.stem: A 50-year-old with vague abdominal pain has been treated for multiple gastric and duodenal ulcers.
items.explanation: Multiple or recurrent peptic ulcers suggest Zollinger–Ellison syndrome from a gastrinoma.

items.stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of loss of consciousness, sweating and dizziness, and eats large amounts of food.
items.explanation: Fasting hypoglycaemia relieved by eating (Whipple triad) with weight gain is an insulinoma.

items.stem: A patient has chronic malnutrition and says food always passes completely undigested.
items.explanation: Steatorrhoea and maldigestion are exocrine failure from chronic pancreatitis.

items.stem: A patient with a previously treated liver hydatid cyst has upper abdominal pain; imaging shows an additional cyst in the pancreas.
items.explanation: A pancreatic cyst in a patient with liver hydatid disease is a pancreatic hydatid cyst.

items.stem: A patient with gallstones for 10 years has recurrent upper abdominal pain and maldigestion.
items.explanation: Recurrent attacks of gallstone pancreatitis can progress to chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency.

items.stem: A patient has upper abdominal pain and fever. CT shows a markedly dilated main pancreatic duct with a filling defect.
items.explanation: A markedly dilated main duct with filling defects (mucin) is a main-duct IPMN; it has high malignant potential and needs resection.

new.stem: A young woman has recurrent palpitations, headache and sweating. Her BP is 185 mmHg systolic despite a calcium channel blocker, an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: Paroxysms of headache, palpitations and sweating with resistant hypertension is phaeochromocytoma.

new.stem: A young woman has recurrent palpitations, headache and sweating. Her BP is 185 mmHg systolic despite a calcium channel blocker, an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
new.explanation: Plasma free (or 24-h urinary fractionated) metanephrines are the biochemical test; imaging (CT/MRI) follows.

new.stem: A young woman has recurrent palpitations, headache and sweating. Her BP is 185 mmHg systolic despite a calcium channel blocker, an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic. Which drug should NOT be used (first) in this condition?
new.explanation: A beta-blocker alone before alpha-blockade leaves alpha stimulation unopposed and can cause a hypertensive crisis; alpha-block first.

items.stem: A child has bile-stained vomiting. What is the best initial imaging?
items.explanation: Bilious vomiting needs an urgent upper GI contrast study to show the DJ flexure and exclude malrotation with volvulus.

items.stem: A patient has a hydroureter but no stone is seen. Which study is best for diagnosis?
items.explanation: Urography (IVU, or CT urography today) shows the level and cause of ureteric obstruction such as a stricture or filling defect.

items.stem: A patient has rectal bleeding, weight loss and a rectal mass on DRE. Which test best shows the depth of invasion?
items.explanation: Endorectal ultrasound (or pelvic MRI) gives local T staging of rectal cancer.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has a 6-cm solitary liver mass found on an infertility ultrasound.
items.explanation: A solid liver lesion is characterised by multiphase (triphasic) contrast CT or MRI.

items.stem: A 2-month-old has episodes of crying, an empty right iliac fossa and a sausage-shaped mass. Which test is diagnostic and therapeutic?
items.explanation: Intussusception is confirmed on ultrasound and reduced by air or contrast enema (diagnostic and therapeutic).

items.stem: A 22-year-old student develops mild jaundice during exam stress. LFTs and haemoglobin are normal; bilirubin is unconjugated and rises with fasting.
items.explanation: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia worsened by fasting or stress is Gilbert syndrome; no treatment needed.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has painless progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and weight loss, with a palpable non-tender gallbladder.
items.explanation: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier law) suggests carcinoma of the pancreatic head.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has fatigue, nausea and yellow eyes for a week; ALT and AST exceed 1000 IU/L. Two colleagues have a similar illness.
items.explanation: Very high transaminases with a cluster of cases is acute viral hepatitis (hepatitis A).

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

items.stem: Episodes of hypertension, sweating and palpitations.
items.explanation: Paroxysmal hypertension, sweating and palpitations is phaeochromocytoma.

items.stem: Resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia.
items.explanation: Resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia is primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome).

items.stem: Central obesity, striae and a buffalo hump.
items.explanation: Central obesity, purple striae and a buffalo hump are Cushing syndrome.

items.stem: A patient with lung cancer has bilateral adrenal masses on CT; they secrete no hormones.
items.explanation: Bilateral non-functioning adrenal masses in lung cancer are metastases (the adrenal is a common site).

items.stem: A woman has an incidental 2-cm non-secreting adrenal mass on CT.
items.explanation: A small (< 4 cm), non-functioning, homogeneous adrenal incidentaloma is an adenoma; follow-up only.

items.stem: Fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain and a dilated bile duct.
items.explanation: Charcot triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) with a dilated duct is ascending cholangitis.

items.stem: Jaundice with a dilated bile duct on ultrasound, but the stone is in the gallbladder.
items.explanation: A stone impacted in the gallbladder neck compressing the common hepatic duct is Mirizzi syndrome.

items.stem: Jaundice with dilated intrahepatic ducts and a contracted gallbladder on ultrasound.
items.explanation: Intrahepatic dilatation with a collapsed gallbladder means a hilar block: cholangiocarcinoma.

items.stem: A patient on chemotherapy develops jaundice, fever and right upper quadrant pain.
items.explanation: Jaundice during chemotherapy without biliary dilatation suggests drug-induced hepatitis.

items.stem: A patient has jaundice and a dilated common bile duct on ultrasound.
items.explanation: Jaundice with a dilated CBD most commonly means a CBD stone (choledocholithiasis).

items.stem: A 30-year-old nurse has jaundice, hepatomegaly and ALT and AST > 1000 IU/L.
items.explanation: Transaminases > 1000 in a healthcare worker suggest acute viral hepatitis (hepatitis B from needlestick).

items.stem: A woman with gallstones for 4 years has acute abdominal pain for 24 h; the CBD is normal but ALP is raised.
items.explanation: A raised ALP with a normal CBD in a patient with gallstones suggests extrinsic CHD compression by a stone in Hartmann pouch (Mirizzi).

items.stem: A 40-year-old diabetic man has slightly raised ALT and AST (about 93 IU/L).
items.explanation: Mildly raised transaminases in a diabetic (metabolic syndrome) is most often non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

items.stem: A patient with renal cell carcinoma has a 7-cm liver mass on ultrasound.
items.explanation: A liver mass in a patient with a known primary cancer is most likely a metastasis; Stauffer syndrome causes abnormal LFTs without metastases.

items.stem: A middle-aged man has painless jaundice, weight loss and a palpable, non-tender, distended gallbladder.
items.explanation: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder means distal biliary obstruction by tumour (distal cholangiocarcinoma or pancreatic head cancer).

new.stem: A 39-year-old woman with asymptomatic gallstones for 4 years has severe upper abdominal pain for 24 hours with nausea and vomiting, still painful despite NSAIDs and opiates. LFTs are normal. All of the following are expected EXCEPT:
options: Hyperaesthesia below the right scapula (Boas sign)
new.explanation: Acute cholecystitis gives a thick-walled gallbladder, raised CRP and leucocytosis (not leucopenia); the CBD is normal.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: A 39-year-old woman with asymptomatic gallstones for 4 years has severe upper abdominal pain for 24 hours with nausea and vomiting, still painful despite NSAIDs and opiates. LFTs are normal. What is the best treatment option now?
options: Conservative treatment, then surgery after 6 weeks
new.explanation: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 h–1 week) is recommended for acute cholecystitis in fit patients (NICE).

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: A 39-year-old woman with asymptomatic gallstones for 4 years has severe upper abdominal pain for 24 hours with nausea and vomiting, still painful despite NSAIDs and opiates. LFTs are normal. Five days after a difficult operation the drain shows 800 mL/day of bile-stained fluid. Which is NOT a likely cause?
options: Leak from a duct of Luschka
new.explanation: Bile in the drain means a leak (cystic stump, duct of Luschka, bile-duct or duodenal injury); cholestasis does not cause bile leakage.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: A 39-year-old woman with asymptomatic gallstones for 4 years has severe upper abdominal pain for 24 hours with nausea and vomiting, still painful despite NSAIDs and opiates. LFTs are normal. What is the best treatment now?
new.explanation: A post-cholecystectomy bile leak with a drain in place is treated by ERCP with sphincterotomy and stent; major duct injury needs MRCP and repair.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: A young woman has right iliac fossa pain, low-grade fever, anorexia and dysuria, and is diagnosed with appendicitis. Which test is 100% reliable for diagnosing appendicitis?
new.explanation: Imaging and scores support the diagnosis, but only direct inspection at laparoscopy with histology confirms it.

new.stem: A young woman has right iliac fossa pain, low-grade fever, anorexia and dysuria, and is diagnosed with appendicitis. Given the presentation, where is the appendix?
new.explanation: A pelvic appendix lies against the bladder and causes dysuria and frequency (and diarrhoea if near the rectum).

new.stem: A young woman has right iliac fossa pain, low-grade fever, anorexia and dysuria, and is diagnosed with appendicitis. Which investigation will you request?
new.explanation: The white-cell count (leucocytosis with left shift) is part of the Alvarado score; urinalysis and a pregnancy test are also essential.

new.stem: Which two Alvarado (MANTRELS) criteria each score 2 points?
options: Right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis
new.explanation: RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2 each; migration, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, rebound, fever and left shift score 1 (total 10).

new.stem: Which is NOT an advantage of laparoscopic over open appendicectomy?
options: Shorter stay and earlier return to work
Allows inspection of the pelvis and other diagnoses
new.explanation: Laparoscopy reduces pain, wound infection and stay and is diagnostic; the intra-abdominal abscess rate is not lower (it may be slightly higher).

new.stem: Which clinical triad defines ascending cholangitis?
options: Fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain
Jaundice, palpable gallbladder and weight loss
Right upper quadrant pain, vomiting and positive Murphy sign
new.explanation: Charcot triad is fever/rigors, jaundice and RUQ pain; adding hypotension and confusion gives Reynolds pentad (suppurative cholangitis).

new.stem: Which vaccines should be given around splenectomy?
options: Pneumococcal, Haemophilus influenzae b, meningococcal (ACWY and B) and annual influenza
No vaccines if lifelong penicillin is taken
new.explanation: Give pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal ACWY and B plus yearly influenza, 2 weeks before elective or 2 weeks after emergency splenectomy.

new.stem: A 71-year-old male smoker with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has felt a pulsating abdominal mass with dull pain radiating to the back for 2 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: A pulsatile, expansile abdominal mass with back pain in an elderly hypertensive smoker is an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

new.stem: A 71-year-old male smoker with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has felt a pulsating abdominal mass with dull pain radiating to the back for 2 months. What is the gold-standard diagnostic test?
new.explanation: Ultrasound screens and follows AAA, but CT angiography defines size, extent and neck anatomy for repair planning.

new.stem: A 71-year-old male smoker with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has felt a pulsating abdominal mass with dull pain radiating to the back for 2 months. He suddenly develops pain in the right leg with an absent dorsalis pedis pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: Sudden pain with a lost pulse is acute limb ischaemia, here from embolism of aneurysm thrombus.

new.stem: A 71-year-old male smoker with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has felt a pulsating abdominal mass with dull pain radiating to the back for 2 months. What is the first-line management of this complication?
new.explanation: Give IV unfractionated heparin immediately to stop clot propagation, then embolectomy or thrombolysis according to limb viability.

new.stem: A mother brings her baby boy because of an abnormal downward urinary stream. The urethral opening is not in its normal position. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: A ventral ectopic meatus with a downward stream is hypospadias (often with chordee and a dorsal hooded foreskin).

new.stem: A mother brings her baby boy because of an abnormal downward urinary stream. The urethral opening is not in its normal position. Which associated abnormality is most common?
new.explanation: Undescended testis (≈ 10%) and inguinal hernia are the commonest associations; with both hypospadias and impalpable testes, exclude a DSD.

new.stem: A mother brings her baby boy because of an abnormal downward urinary stream. The urethral opening is not in its normal position. What is the most common complication after surgical repair?
new.explanation: Urethrocutaneous fistula is the commonest complication of hypospadias repair; meatal stenosis and stricture also occur.

new.stem: A 61-year-old man has frequency, hesitancy and a weak stream. DRE shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate. He has also had erectile dysfunction for 6 months. What is the first-line management?
new.explanation: Tadalafil 5 mg daily treats both LUTS from BPH and erectile dysfunction; an alpha-blocker is first-line when ED is absent.

new.stem: Eight years later his PSA is 16 ng/mL and the prostate is nodular and irregular. He has localised adenocarcinoma, Gleason 4+4, with no metastasis. What is the best treatment?
new.explanation: High-risk localised prostate cancer in a fit man is treated radically: radical prostatectomy, or radiotherapy with long-term ADT.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has an incidental 3-cm enhancing mass in the upper pole of the kidney on CT; PET is negative.
items.explanation: A small (T1a, ≤ 4 cm) renal cell carcinoma is treated by nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman with chronic infections and recurrent stones has a left kidney contributing < 5% of total function on MAG3.
items.explanation: A non-functioning, chronically infected kidney is removed by simple nephrectomy.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man on IV antibiotics for 5 days has fever, rigors and flank pain; HR 120, BP 80/60. CT shows hydroureteronephrosis to the mid-ureter.
items.explanation: An infected obstructed kidney with septic shock needs urgent decompression; percutaneous nephrostomy is safest in the unstable patient.

items.stem: A 4-year-old girl has recurrent febrile UTIs despite long-term antibiotics; micturating cystogram shows a dilated, tortuous left ureter.
items.explanation: High-grade vesicoureteric reflux with breakthrough febrile UTIs is treated by ureteric reimplantation.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has painless haematuria; CT shows a tumour of the left renal pelvis without metastasis.
items.explanation: Upper-tract urothelial carcinoma is treated by nephroureterectomy with a bladder cuff.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has dysuria, frequency and suprapubic pain without fever or flank pain. Urine is cloudy with leucocytes and nitrites.
items.explanation: Lower urinary symptoms without fever or loin pain are acute (uncomplicated) cystitis.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has fever, chills and perineal pain; DRE is difficult because of severe anterior rectal tenderness. Urine grows E. coli.
items.explanation: Fever, perineal pain and an exquisitely tender prostate is acute bacterial prostatitis (avoid prostatic massage).

items.stem: A 28-year-old diabetic woman has high fever, flank pain, vomiting and renal angle tenderness. CT shows pockets of gas and fluid in the left kidney.
items.explanation: Gas within the renal parenchyma in a diabetic is emphysematous pyelonephritis: antibiotics, drainage, sometimes nephrectomy.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: An elderly man has haematuria; ultrasound shows a 2-cm tumour in the bladder. What is the next step?
new.explanation: A bladder mass needs cystoscopy and transurethral resection for histology and staging; CT urography assesses the upper tracts.

new.stem: An elderly man has haematuria; ultrasound shows a 2-cm tumour in the bladder. What is the treatment?
new.explanation: TURBT is diagnostic and therapeutic for non-muscle-invasive tumours; intravesical therapy follows according to risk.

new.stem: A 25-year-old woman had a difficult caesarean section for bleeding. Ten days later she has severe right flank pain; ultrasound shows severe hydroureteronephrosis down to the pelvis with no stones. Which test best establishes the cause of obstruction?
new.explanation: CT urography (or antegrade/retrograde study) shows the level of a ligated or injured ureter and any urinoma.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: A 25-year-old woman had a difficult caesarean section for bleeding. Ten days later she has severe right flank pain; ultrasound shows severe hydroureteronephrosis down to the pelvis with no stones. Ureteric ligation is suspected. All of the following are initial options EXCEPT:
new.explanation: Initial care is resuscitation, antibiotics and drainage (nephrostomy or retrograde stent); delayed reimplantation repairs it. Nephrectomy is not indicated.

why: Added from 39th batch End-induction Block A (recalled exam)

new.stem: A 4-year-old boy has left lower abdominal pain and is underweight. Ultrasound shows hydronephrosis and urinalysis shows mild painless pyuria. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
new.explanation: PUJ obstruction is confirmed on urography (IVU, CT or MR urography) and a diuretic renogram; ureteroscopy has no role.

new.stem: A 4-year-old boy has left lower abdominal pain and is underweight. Ultrasound shows hydronephrosis and urinalysis shows mild painless pyuria. Which is the best test of split renal function and drainage?
new.explanation: A MAG3 diuretic renogram measures differential function and confirms obstruction; DMSA shows scarring and static function.

new.stem: A 4-year-old boy has left lower abdominal pain and is underweight. Ultrasound shows hydronephrosis and urinalysis shows mild painless pyuria. What is the best long-term management?
new.explanation: Symptomatic PUJ obstruction or falling function is treated by dismembered (Anderson–Hynes) pyeloplasty; nephrectomy only for a non-functioning kidney.

new.stem: A 68-year-old man arrives in the emergency department with abdominal pain and a distended bladder. Which is the correct technique for male urethral catheterisation?
options: Aseptic technique, lidocaine gel, penis held upright, insert to the hub and see urine before inflating the balloon
Inflate the balloon as soon as resistance is felt
Use the largest catheter to overcome resistance
Insert only half the catheter length, then inflate
new.explanation: Insert the catheter fully to the bifurcation and inflate only once urine drains, so the balloon cannot be inflated in the urethra.

new.stem: A 68-year-old man arrives in the emergency department with abdominal pain and a distended bladder. The catheter is passed but no urine drains. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Check the position: advance fully, flush with sterile saline and confirm a full bladder (scan) before inflating
Remove it and force a larger catheter
Insert a suprapubic catheter at once
new.explanation: No urine means the catheter is in the urethra, blocked by gel, or the bladder is empty; check, flush and scan before inflating.

new.stem: A patient needs a Foley catheter and develops haematuria during insertion. What is the most likely cause of the bleeding?
options: Urethral trauma (false passage or balloon inflated in the urethra)
new.explanation: Bleeding at catheterisation is usually urethral trauma (false passage) or a balloon inflated in the prostatic urethra.

new.stem: A patient needs a Foley catheter and develops haematuria during insertion. How should it be managed?
options: Stop, deflate and remove; then one gentle attempt by a senior/urologist (coudé tip) or a suprapubic catheter
new.explanation: Stop, deflate and withdraw; if retention persists use a suprapubic catheter or urology-guided catheterisation, and check Hb and urine.

new.stem: A 72-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has acute urinary retention and severe suprapubic pain; bladder scan shows 900 mL. Which is the most common complication of a long-term indwelling catheter?
new.explanation: Bacteriuria and CAUTI are universal with long-term catheters; encrustation, blockage, stricture and stones also occur.

new.stem: A 72-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has acute urinary retention and severe suprapubic pain; bladder scan shows 900 mL. Which is an absolute contraindication to urethral catheterisation?
options: Suspected urethral injury (blood at the meatus, pelvic fracture)
new.explanation: Suspected urethral injury (blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate) contraindicates urethral catheterisation; a suprapubic catheter is used.

new.stem: Haematuria develops after Foley catheter insertion. What are the likely causes?
options: Urethral trauma or balloon inflated in the urethra
new.explanation: Bleeding at catheterisation is usually urethral trauma (false passage) or a balloon inflated in the prostatic urethra.

new.stem: Haematuria develops after Foley catheter insertion. How is it managed?
options: Stop, deflate and remove; then one gentle attempt by a senior/urologist (coudé tip) or a suprapubic catheter
new.explanation: Stop, deflate and withdraw; if retention persists use a suprapubic catheter or urology-guided catheterisation.

new.stem: A 75-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart failure (EF 40%) was caught in a house fire when his clothes ignited. He has extensive white, leathery burns of the arms and legs with red blistered margins; pulse 110/min, BP 90/60 mmHg. What is the best initial management?
options: Airway assessment and IV fluid resuscitation
new.explanation: Burns follow ATLS: secure the airway (inhalation risk) and start IV resuscitation; dressings and surgery come later.

new.stem: A 75-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart failure (EF 40%) was caught in a house fire when his clothes ignited. He has extensive white, leathery burns of the arms and legs with red blistered margins; pulse 110/min, BP 90/60 mmHg. What is the depth of these burns?
new.explanation: White, leathery, painless skin is full-thickness burn; the red blistered margins are partial thickness.

new.stem: A 75-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart failure (EF 40%) was caught in a house fire when his clothes ignited. He has extensive white, leathery burns of the arms and legs with red blistered margins; pulse 110/min, BP 90/60 mmHg. What is the most common complication in the first 24 hours?
new.explanation: Capillary leak causes hypovolaemic burn shock in the first 24–48 h; sepsis and contractures come later.

new.stem: A 75-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart failure (EF 40%) was caught in a house fire when his clothes ignited. He has extensive white, leathery burns of the arms and legs with red blistered margins; pulse 110/min, BP 90/60 mmHg. Given his diabetes and heart failure, what is the key consideration in fluid resuscitation?
options: Use the standard formula without change
Start Parkland cautiously and titrate to urine output
new.explanation: Parkland is only a starting point; titrate to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h to avoid both under-resuscitation and fluid overload in heart failure.

new.stem: A 45-year-old man is brought after a car crash. The right chest moves paradoxically with bruising, reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds. He is conscious but distressed; BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO2 86%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
new.explanation: Paradoxical movement of a chest segment after blunt trauma is flail chest (two or more ribs broken in two or more places).

new.stem: A 45-year-old man is brought after a car crash. The right chest moves paradoxically with bruising, reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds. He is conscious but distressed; BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO2 86%. Which mechanism mainly compromises his lungs?
new.explanation: Hypoxia in flail chest is caused mainly by the underlying pulmonary contusion, aggravated by pain-limited ventilation.

new.stem: A 45-year-old man is brought after a car crash. The right chest moves paradoxically with bruising, reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds. He is conscious but distressed; BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO2 86%. Chest X-ray and CT show a massive haemothorax. What is the next immediate step?
new.explanation: Massive haemothorax is treated with a large-bore chest drain and resuscitation; thoracotomy if > 1500 mL initially or > 200 mL/h.

new.stem: A 45-year-old man is brought after a car crash. The right chest moves paradoxically with bruising, reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds. He is conscious but distressed; BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO2 86%. He improves but remains hypoxic with paradoxical movement. What is the next definitive step?
new.explanation: Persistent hypoxia despite analgesia and oxygen needs intubation and ventilation (internal splinting); rib fixation is increasingly used to wean.

new.stem: An elderly patient has headache 3 weeks after a minor head injury; CT shows a crescent-shaped collection. What is the diagnosis?
new.explanation: A crescentic (hypodense) collection weeks after minor trauma in an elderly patient is a chronic subdural haematoma: burr-hole drainage.

new.stem: A man cuts his forearm on glass; the wound is not deep and its edges are everted. Which closure and immediate drug are most appropriate?
options: Simple interrupted non-absorbable monofilament (e.g. 4/0 nylon) sutures and tetanus prophylaxis
Absorbable braided sutures and IV antibiotics
Leave open and give oral steroids
new.explanation: Superficial lacerations are closed with interrupted non-absorbable monofilament sutures; check tetanus status and give prophylaxis.

new.stem: A man cuts his forearm on glass; the wound is not deep and its edges are everted. If the wound is deep, how should it be closed?
options: Layered closure: absorbable subcutaneous sutures, then skin sutures
Leave open to heal by secondary intention
new.explanation: Deep wounds need layered closure with absorbable (e.g. polyglactin) deep sutures to close dead space and reduce tension, haematoma and infection.

new.stem: A 28-year-old man is brought after a road traffic accident with a deep right-thigh laceration and pulsatile bleeding. He is pale and anxious; BP 85/60 mmHg, HR 130/min. What type of bleeding is this?
options: Arterial: bright red and spurting in time with the pulse
new.explanation: Arterial bleeding is bright red and pulsatile; venous bleeding is dark and flows steadily. Control with direct pressure or a tourniquet.

new.stem: A 28-year-old man is brought after a road traffic accident with a deep right-thigh laceration and pulsatile bleeding. He is pale and anxious; BP 85/60 mmHg, HR 130/min. What is the maximum safe tourniquet time?
options: No limit if the limb is cooled
new.explanation: Limit tourniquet time to about 2 h (record it); complications are nerve palsy, ischaemia, compartment syndrome and reperfusion injury.

new.stem: A sedated, intubated patient in the ICU needs a nasogastric tube. What is the most dangerous complication of insertion?
new.explanation: In a sedated, intubated patient the tube can pass into the airway unnoticed (no cough reflex); feeding into the lung is the danger.

new.stem: A sedated, intubated patient in the ICU needs a nasogastric tube. After NG insertion and feeding he becomes hypotensive and desaturates with secretions around the mouth and tube. What happened?
options: Aspiration of feed into the lungs
new.explanation: This is aspiration: stop feeds and suction. Prevent it by checking aspirate pH ≤ 5.5 or X-ray before feeding and nursing 30–45° head-up.

new.stem: A 72-year-old sedated, ventilated ICU patient needs an NG tube. What are the possible complications and how are they minimised?
new.explanation: Misplacement into the airway is the major danger; confirm placement (pH ≤ 5.5 or X-ray) before use.

new.stem: A 72-year-old sedated, ventilated ICU patient needs an NG tube. After feeding he desaturates with secretions. What happened and what is the immediate management?
options: Aspiration of feed into the lungs
new.explanation: Aspiration: stop feeds, suction and oxygen; confirm tube position before feeding.

new.stem: A 65-year-old man with distension, persistent vomiting and absent bowel sounds has intestinal obstruction; an NG tube is ordered for decompression. How is NG tube placement confirmed?
options: Aspirate pH ≤ 5.5, or chest X-ray if no aspirate or pH is high
Bubbling when the end is placed in water
Litmus paper colour change to blue
new.explanation: Use gastric aspirate pH ≤ 5.5 first-line and X-ray if that fails; the whoosh and bubble tests are unreliable and unsafe.

new.stem: A 65-year-old man with distension, persistent vomiting and absent bowel sounds has intestinal obstruction; an NG tube is ordered for decompression. Which is a contraindication to NG tube insertion?
new.explanation: Basal skull or severe mid-face fractures risk intracranial passage, so use the orogastric route; recent oesophageal surgery or atresia are others.

items.stem: An elderly woman becomes confused 2 days after surgery; plasma osmolality is low.
items.explanation: Postoperative confusion with low osmolality is hyponatraemia (ADH response plus hypotonic fluids).

items.stem: A man with extensive muscle destruction has tall peaked T waves on ECG.
items.explanation: Rhabdomyolysis releases potassium; peaked T waves signal hyperkalaemia (give IV calcium first).

items.stem: A man has prominent U waves on ECG.
items.explanation: U waves, flat T waves and ST depression are signs of hypokalaemia.

items.stem: A malnourished alcoholic given fluids and nutrition has hypokalaemia that does not correct despite repeated potassium infusions.
items.explanation: Refractory hypokalaemia means hypomagnesaemia (renal K loss); replace magnesium first (and watch for refeeding).

items.stem: A soil-contaminated open fracture from a farm accident develops, days later, rapidly spreading swelling, severe pain, systemic toxicity and sepsis.
items.explanation: Rapid spreading swelling and toxicity in a soil-contaminated wound is clostridial gas gangrene: radical debridement, penicillin, clindamycin.

items.stem: After multiple long-bone fractures a patient develops, within 24–72 hours, respiratory distress, confusion and a petechial rash.
items.explanation: Hypoxia, neurological signs and petechiae 1–3 days after long-bone fractures is fat embolism syndrome.

items.stem: A 19-year-old athlete with a tibial fracture has worsening pain hours later, worse on passive dorsiflexion; distal pulses are present.
items.explanation: Pain out of proportion and on passive stretch is compartment syndrome; pulses persist until late. Urgent fasciotomy.

items.stem: A superficial 14 × 10 cm burn wound of the back, after debridement, with a healthy vascular bed and no exposed structures.
items.explanation: A large wound with a healthy vascular bed is covered by split-thickness skin graft.

items.stem: A small nasal ala defect after skin cancer excision needs excellent contour and minimal contraction.
items.explanation: Full-thickness grafts contract little and match facial skin, so suit small facial defects (local flaps are an alternative).

items.stem: A fingertip wound < 1 cm with no exposed bone.
items.explanation: Small fingertip wounds without exposed bone heal well by secondary intention.

items.stem: A cheek defect closed by rotating a flap around a known vascular pedicle.
items.explanation: A flap based on a named vessel is an axial-pattern flap.

items.stem: A 24-year-old has an avulsion over the anterior tibia; after debridement bone without periosteum is exposed and the surrounding tissue is traumatised and previously irradiated.
items.explanation: Bare bone cannot take a graft and the local tissue is unusable, so a free muscle flap brings well-vascularised cover.

items.stem: A 65-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve and infective endocarditis suddenly has a cold, pale, pulseless right leg with sensory loss below the knee; motor function is intact.
items.explanation: Sudden pain, pallor and pulselessness from an embolus is acute limb ischaemia; with intact motor function the limb is salvageable.

items.stem: A patient has absent femoral pulses, buttock claudication and erectile dysfunction.
items.explanation: Aorto-iliac occlusion gives Leriche syndrome: buttock claudication, impotence and absent femoral pulses.

items.stem: A patient develops pain and a tense swollen leg after emergency embolectomy.
items.explanation: Reperfusion after revascularisation causes oedema and compartment syndrome: fasciotomy.

items.stem: A 30-year-old male smoker has ischaemia of the distal digits and previous superficial thrombophlebitis.
items.explanation: Distal ischaemia with migratory thrombophlebitis in a young smoker is Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans).

items.stem: An asthmatic patient with wheeze needs ureteroscopic stone extraction.
items.explanation: Spinal anaesthesia avoids airway instrumentation (bronchospasm) and suits ureteroscopy.

items.stem: A patient with COPD needs emergency laparotomy for a perforated viscus.
items.explanation: Emergency laparotomy (full stomach) needs GA with rapid-sequence intubation to protect the airway.

items.stem: A patient with heart failure and CKD needs elective inguinal hernia repair.
items.explanation: Open inguinal hernia repair under local anaesthesia (± sedation) avoids GA risks in high-risk patients.

items.stem: Wide local excision of a basal cell carcinoma of the cheek.
items.explanation: Small facial skin excisions are done under local anaesthesia ± sedation.

items.stem: An elderly woman has inoperable oesophageal cancer with severe dysphagia.
items.explanation: Inoperable oesophageal cancer needs long-term enteral access below the block: gastrostomy (or stent).

items.stem: A man is stable after uncomplicated herniorrhaphy with normal bowel sounds.
items.explanation: After uncomplicated surgery, early oral feeding is resumed.

items.stem: A patient has undergone a Whipple procedure.
items.explanation: A feeding jejunostomy placed at pancreaticoduodenectomy allows early enteral feeding beyond the anastomoses.

items.stem: A patient with multiple fractures has prolonged ileus.
items.explanation: A non-functioning gut (prolonged ileus) needs parenteral nutrition.

items.stem: A patient with severe trauma and a liver injury.
items.explanation: Critically ill trauma patients should start early enteral (nasogastric) feeding within 24–48 h if the gut works.

new.stem: A barium swallow is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
new.explanation: A grossly dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly at the cardia (bird beak) is achalasia.

new.stem: An erect chest X-ray is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
new.explanation: Free gas under both hemidiaphragms on an erect film means pneumoperitoneum, usually a perforated viscus.

new.stem: A plain abdominal X-ray of a distended elderly patient is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
new.explanation: A huge inverted-U (coffee-bean) loop arising from the pelvis is sigmoid volvulus.

new.stem: A contrast CT of the upper abdomen of a febrile patient is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
new.explanation: A large hypodense collection with an enhancing wall and necrotic debris in the right lobe is a liver abscess.

new.stem: An erect abdominal X-ray is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
new.explanation: Multiple central air–fluid levels in dilated small-bowel loops indicate small bowel obstruction.

new.stem: A plain abdominal X-ray is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
new.explanation: Speckled calcification across the line of the pancreas (L1–L2) is chronic calcific pancreatitis.

new.stem: A barium swallow of a patient with progressive dysphagia and weight loss is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
new.explanation: An irregular stricture with shouldering and proximal dilatation is oesophageal carcinoma.

new.stem: An MRCP of a jaundiced patient is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
new.explanation: Filling defects within a dilated common bile duct on MRCP are CBD stones.
